title: Area IV review: Preflight Lesson on a Maneuver to be Performed in Flight
intro: One Task, twelve questions: the maneuver briefing an evaluator asks you to deliver. They mix purpose, elements and errors, completion standards, risk and teaching methods, using slow flight and ground reference maneuvers as the sample maneuvers.

questions.q: You are briefing slow flight to a 10-hour learner. After yesterday's flight your notes show deviations of altitude plus or minus 70 feet, heading plus or minus 8 degrees, airspeed plus 7 and minus 0 knots, and bank plus or minus 8 degrees. Which statement is accurate, and what do you tell the learner today?
options: The numbers are inside the private and commercial tolerances and miss only the CFI tolerance, so the learner is almost ready for the checkride standard
The airspeed is outside the private tolerance, because the private ACS allows only plus 5 and minus 0 knots
The numbers are inside the private tolerances on all four items but outside the commercial and CFI tolerances for altitude, airspeed and bank, so they fit this stage and set the next target
The numbers are inside all three tolerance sets, because the heading deviation of 8 degrees is within the plus or minus 10 degrees all three share
questions.why: Private slow flight standards are altitude plus or minus 100 feet, heading plus or minus 10 degrees, airspeed plus 10 and minus 0 knots, and bank plus or minus 10 degrees (ACS PA.VII.A.S5). All four of the learner's numbers fit. Commercial and CFI are altitude plus or minus 50 feet, airspeed plus 5 and minus 0 knots and bank plus or minus 5 degrees (ACS CA.VII.A.S5, AI.X.A.S5); 70 feet, plus 7 knots and 8 degrees all miss those, and only the heading fits. The +5/-0 knot limit is not the private one. Assessment uses standards suitably modified for the learner's stage [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and lesson standards grow toward the ACS over time [[25:171|AIH 9-1]].

questions.q: You plan to brief a rectangular course and have chosen 1,000 feet AGL, the top of the usual 600 to 1,000 foot range. The map shows a 640-foot AGL radio tower about 1,500 feet from the nearest leg of your planned track. What do you brief?
options: Neither clearance is met: 1,000 feet gives only 360 feet above the tower, short of 500 feet, and 1,500 feet is short of 2,000 feet horizontally, so move the maneuver away from the tower
It is fine, because 1,000 feet AGL is inside the 600 to 1,000 foot range the AFH gives for ground reference maneuvers
Drop to 600 feet AGL so the airplane passes well below the top of the tower
Keep 1,000 feet AGL and tell the learner to watch the tower, since obstruction clearance applies only to the maneuver altitude
questions.why: The AFH lists obstruction clearance of no less than 500 feet vertically above the obstruction and 2,000 feet horizontally as one of the things to weigh when choosing the altitude [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Here 1,000 minus 640 is 360 feet, under 500 feet, and 1,500 feet is under 2,000 feet, so both are missed. The 600 to 1,000 foot range is a general guide and does not override the clearance. Dropping to 600 feet is worse: it would put the airplane lower than the tower top and cut engine-out time and glide distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Brief the obstruction as a hazard and pick a better area or location (R1).

questions.q: Just before your ground brief on slow flight and stalls, a 10-hour learner says: "I have to finish this stage today, my job interview is Friday and my schedule is full." He is rushing and tense. Which risk category is this, and what does the AIH tell you to do?
options: Pilot: treat it as an IMSAFE item and brief faster so the lesson still fits the time
Environment: nothing to do, because only weather and terrain count as hazards for a maneuver brief
Aircraft: nothing to do, because time pressure affects only the learner's own preparation
External pressure: acknowledge the schedule, say changes are fine, and be ready to move to classroom instruction or end the lesson early if he stays apprehensive
questions.why: PAVE groups risk into pilot, aircraft, environment and external pressures [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Schedule and job demands are external pressures, which the AIH calls the most insidious hazards. Instructors should ease the concerns, stress that schedule changes are acceptable, and be ready to change from airplane to classroom instruction or end the lesson early if the learner seems apprehensive about time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Rushing the brief makes the unprepared-learner hazard worse [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

questions.q: While planning a rectangular course brief, you list the hazard "engine failure at 700 feet AGL over fields you have not looked at" and rate it occasional likelihood and critical severity. Using the RMH matrix, what do you do?
options: The risk is medium (green), so it is a go and no further mitigation is needed
The risk is serious (yellow), so it is a no-go until you add a mitigation and the next assessment shows medium or low
The risk is serious (yellow), which only means extra caution, so fly as planned and accept it
The risk is high (red) only if the learner is below 20 hours; otherwise it is acceptable
questions.why: The RMH gives this exact case: critical severity with occasional likelihood is serious (yellow), and high (red) or serious (yellow) imply no-go unless you find a way to reduce the risk so the next assessment shows medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. For this hazard the AFH mitigation is to look at the area and have one or more emergency landing locations [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Reassess if the field or conditions change (obsolescence) [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. After mitigation you consciously accept what remains while guarding the controls [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

questions.q: The evaluator asks why you will describe the common errors of the maneuver on the ground, before the first flight, instead of letting a new learner find each one in the air. Which teaching principle best supports briefing them first?
options: Recency: things learned most recently are best remembered, so the errors should be covered last, in the postflight
Intensity: a dramatic experience teaches more than a routine one, so the errors should be a surprise
Exercise: connections strengthen with practice, so the errors are best learned by repeating them in flight
Primacy: what is learned first leaves a strong, almost unshakable impression, and faulty habits are hard to correct, so the first attempts should go the right way
questions.why: Primacy says what is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression, which is why the instructor must teach correctly the first time [[25:64|AIH 3-13]]. Learners need to perform the maneuver the right way the first few times to set a good habit, and faulty habits are difficult to correct [[25:126|AIH 5-23]]. Recency supports a summary at the end, not first exposure. The AIH also allows, safety permitting, letting a learner go part way into a mistake [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but that does not replace the brief.

questions.q: After the first rectangular course lesson, your 14-hour learner can describe the legs and turns and explain why the bank must change with groundspeed, but still needs your help to fly the pattern and hold the track. Which learner-centered grade fits?
options: Describe, because the learner still needs assistance to fly it
Practice, because the learner plans and executes the scenario and only needs coaching to fix deviations
Explain, because the learner understands the concepts and principles but needs assistance to execute
Perform, because the learner can state every step without notes
questions.why: Explain means the learner can describe the activity and understand the underlying concepts, principles and procedures, but needs assistance to execute the maneuver [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]. Describe covers only the physical characteristics and cognitive elements. Practice requires planning and executing it, with coaching correcting errors. Perform means no instructor help. Grading is progressive, so a task can move from describe toward practice over later flights [[25:138|AIH 6-7]]. Tell the learner the target level for the next flight.

questions.q: In your slow flight brief you say you will have the learner roll into a level turn at the slow flight speed. What do you tell the learner to expect and do to hold altitude in the turn?
options: Add power during the turn to maintain altitude
Hold the same power and pull back more, since the elevator holds altitude
Reduce power slightly so the angle of attack stays unchanged
Retract the flaps one notch at the start of the turn to reduce drag
questions.why: In slow flight turns it is necessary to increase power to maintain altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. At this speed any further increase in angle of attack, increase in load factor or reduction in power will result in a stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], so more back pressure or less power is the wrong direction. Abrupt flap retraction in slow flight can cause a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Brief the turn as its own element, because the learner who forgets the extra power sees an altitude loss and a stall warning.

questions.q: Your brief covers leaving slow flight in the landing configuration. Which exit sequence do you teach?
options: Raise the flaps first to cut drag, then add power once the airplane is clean

Add power, then apply forward pressure as airspeed and lift increase to hold altitude; stay coordinated, and clean up flaps and gear as airspeed increases while anticipating the angle-of-attack change and retrimming
Lower the nose to build airspeed, then add power when the airspeed is back to cruise
Add power and keep the back pressure so the airplane climbs away from the stall
questions.why: To exit, add power; as airspeed and lift increase, apply forward control pressure to reduce the AOA and maintain altitude, stay coordinated, and clean up as airspeed increases, adjusting trim and anticipating the AOA change as gear and flaps come up to avoid a stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Raising flaps first with no power is the abrupt change the AFH warns can cause a stall. Lowering the nose first loses altitude, and holding back pressure keeps the AOA high [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

questions.q: You brief a rectangular course for a left pattern with the wind from the south. The learner enters on the east leg flying north. On your marker board you ask which turn needs the shallowest bank, rolled in slowly, and ends with less than 90 degrees of heading change. Which turn is it?
options: From the north-flying downwind leg onto the west-flying base leg
From the west-flying base leg onto the south-flying upwind leg
From the east-flying crosswind leg onto the north-flying downwind leg
From the south-flying upwind leg onto the east-flying crosswind leg
questions.why: With a south wind the north-flying leg is the downwind leg. The upwind leg flies south into the wind. The turn from upwind to crosswind is the one the AFH describes: groundspeed is lowest, so a shallow bank rolled in slowly while the crosswind drifts the airplane to the inside; the airplane keeps an angle into the wind toward the outside, so the turn is less than 90 degrees [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. Downwind to base is steep and over 90 degrees. Base to upwind is medium and under 90 degrees but not shallow. Crosswind to downwind is medium and over 90 degrees [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. Roll rate follows drift [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

questions.q: You are briefing why bank must change around the rectangular course. Your airplane flies 100 knots true airspeed, and the wind is 20 knots straight down the downwind leg and straight up the upwind leg. Using radius = V squared / (g x tan bank), with V in feet per second and g = 32.174, you plan a 45 degree bank at the start of the downwind turn. About what bank holds the same ground radius when the groundspeed is lowest on the upwind side?
options: 30 degrees
34 degrees
24 degrees
18 degrees
questions.why: Downwind groundspeed is 120 knots, or 202.5 feet per second. The radius is 202.5 squared divided by (32.174 x tan 45), about 1,275 feet. Upwind groundspeed is 80 knots, or 135.0 feet per second, so tan bank = 135.0 squared / (32.174 x 1,275) = 0.444, and the bank is 24.0 degrees. The answer 30 comes from scaling the bank linearly (45 x 80/120), which overstates it, because tan bank changes with the square of groundspeed. The AFH shows the same pattern: 45 degrees at 100 knots groundspeed needs about 33 degrees at 80 knots [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. Higher groundspeed means steeper bank, lower means shallower [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

questions.q: A school is moving to scenario-based training (SBT). A colleague tells you the new plan format means you no longer need a stand-alone lesson to teach slow flight. What does the AIH say?
options: He is wrong: maneuvers needing repetition are still taught in concentrated settings and then built into realistic flights, and the SBT plan adds scenario, hazards with mitigation and a self-critique-led postflight
He is right: SBT replaces maneuver training, so maneuvers are learned only inside scenarios
He is wrong: the SBT plan allows maneuvers but leaves out completion standards and hazards
He is right only for private pilot training; commercial and CFI training must stay maneuver-based
questions.why: SBT does not preclude traditional maneuver-based training. Flight maneuvers are integrated into scenarios, and those needing repetition are still taught in concentrated settings, then integrated into realistic flight situations [[25:154|AIH 7-10]]. The SBT plan adds a type of training, a scenario, possible hazards with a mitigating strategy, and a postflight review that usually begins with the learner's self-critique; it still carries completion standards [[25:156|AIH 7-12]]. Plan format should be adapted to the learner [[25:153|AIH 7-9]].

questions.q: A 14-hour learner asks, "Why do we spend whole lessons on rectangular courses and turns around a point? I already fly the pattern." Which answer best delivers the purpose of the maneuver (K1) in the brief?
options: Because the private ACS requires ground reference maneuvers and you will be tested on them
Because they are the only way to learn to fly a 45 degree bank, which you need in the pattern
Because flying low over the ground is the best place to practice stall recovery

Because these maneuvers combine the four fundamentals into integrated skills used from every takeoff to every landing, and the rectangular course replicates the traffic pattern, so it prepares you for pattern and landing practice
questions.why: The AFH calls ground reference maneuvers the principal maneuvers that combine the four fundamentals into integrated skills used in everyday flight, from every takeoff to every landing [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. The rectangular course replicates the traffic pattern and prepares the pilot for the pattern and subsequent landing pattern practice [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. "It is on the checkride" is not a purpose; the ACS is a testing document and lessons should not focus on the minimum for passing [[24:30|AFH 1-9]] [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Banks should stay at 45 degrees or less [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], and stall practice is not the purpose.
